Although lymphoma and melanoma incidence increased in this cohort, causality with anakinra remained inconclusive. While no firm guidelines endorse regular screening for these specific cancers in patients receiving IL-1ra therapy, consideration should be given to those with significant risk factors. Initiate IL-1ras for current recommended duration with current therapy wean The advent of steroid-sparing IL-1ras like anakinra and rilonacept has revolutionized chronic recurrent pericarditis (ChRP) treatment. While IL-1ras offer targeted IL-1α/IL-1β pathway inhibition, concerns about long-term malignancy risk affect treatment decisions, especially in those with recent or familial cancer history. The AIRTRIP1and RHAPSODY2clinical trials excluded patients with cancer within the last 5 years, making extrapolation challenging and creating provider and patient uncertainty regarding IL-1ra use in this context. These concerns stem from IL-1’s dual role in cancer biology. While primarily recognized for its protumoral effects, IL-1 may paradoxically inhibit cancer development in certain contexts.3Combined IL-1α/IL-1β inhibition may amplify this effect, yet clinical evidence validating these cellular concerns is lacking.4Fleischmann and colleagues’ review of anakinra in rheumatoid arthritis5suggests a decreased long-term malignancy risk, attributed to reduced systemic inflammation. Although lymphoma and melanoma incidence increased in this cohort, causality with anakinra remained inconclusive. While no firm guidelines endorse regular screening for these specific cancers in patients receiving IL-1ra therapy, consideration should be given to those with significant risk factors. Bilal and colleagues6reviewed cancer risk associated with long-term IL inhibitor use, suggesting an increased risk correlating with treatment duration. Analysis of studies including rilonacept use by Schumacher and colleagues reported isolated cases of prostate cancer and leg squamous cell carcinoma during phase II and III trials.7,8In the RHAPSODY trial,21 case of squamous cell carcinoma was reported. Notably, therapy discontinuation was not necessary for any event. Considering this evidence, malignancy risk does not appear to be significant with long-term IL-1ra use. Generalizability limitations include follow-up duration, as prolonged IL-1 inhibition might trigger cancer in genetically predisposed individuals. While malignancy diagnosis may be limited by follow-up, no malignancies were reported during the open-label study spanning 72 to 96 weeks of rilonacept treatment for cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes.9Whether IL-1ras unmask or cause cancer in such cases or are innocent bystanders would be challenging to address. For patients with prior malignancies, a shared decision-making process with an oncologist is advised. This allows weighing the risks of untreated ChRP against cancer recurrence. Limited data hinder estimating recurrence risk with IL-1ra therapy, particularly in patients with frequent flares. Nevertheless, in certain cases, oncological consultation is invaluable for assessing recurrence risk and increasing confidence in IL-1ra use for suitable patients. However, these recommendations become more diluted in those with a family history of cancer, even with suspected genetic syndromes, as in this patient. If the guidelines for screening of the specific cancers are followed, a reasonable counsel can be provided to the patients in need regarding IL-1ra therapy for treating recurrent pericarditis. Extension of therapy beyond recommended durations, like 18 to 24 months for rilonacept, can be considered on a case-by-case basis depending on the interim development of suspicious lesions found on screening vs the current pericarditis status. Additionally, using prophylactic measures in select cases to prevent the development of malignancies in genetically predisposed individuals may increase confidence in prescribing IL-1ras.10 Further genetic testing did not identify a sequence variation. After a shared decision, rilonacept was started, allowing the patient to taper off ibuprofen and colchicine within 10 weeks with no further symptoms. While taking rilonacept, she increased physical activity and showed reduced pericardial enhancement on cardiac MRI. She has been closely monitored for premalignant conditions, particularly breast and cervical cancer, and has been free of such conditions after 1 year of therapy.

While no firm guidelines endorse regular screening for these specific cancers in patients receiving IL-1ra therapy, consideration should be given to those with significant risk factors. While IL-1ras offer targeted IL-1α/IL-1β pathway inhibition, concerns about long-term malignancy risk affect treatment decisions, especially in those with recent or familial cancer history. The AIRTRIP1and RHAPSODY2clinical trials excluded patients with cancer within the last 5 years, making extrapolation challenging and creating provider and patient uncertainty regarding IL-1ra use in this context. These concerns stem from IL-1’s dual role in cancer biology. While primarily recognized for its protumoral effects, IL-1 may paradoxically inhibit cancer development in certain contexts.3Combined IL-1α/IL-1β inhibition may amplify this effect, yet clinical evidence validating these cellular concerns is lacking.4Fleischmann and colleagues’ review of anakinra in rheumatoid arthritis5suggests a decreased long-term malignancy risk, attributed to reduced systemic inflammation. Although lymphoma and melanoma incidence increased in this cohort, causality with anakinra remained inconclusive. While no firm guidelines endorse regular screening for these specific cancers in patients receiving IL-1ra therapy, consideration should be given to those with significant risk factors. Bilal and colleagues6reviewed cancer risk associated with long-term IL inhibitor use, suggesting an increased risk correlating with treatment duration. Analysis of studies including rilonacept use by Schumacher and colleagues reported isolated cases of prostate cancer and leg squamous cell carcinoma during phase II and III trials.7,8In the RHAPSODY trial,21 case of squamous cell carcinoma was reported. Notably, therapy discontinuation was not necessary for any event. Considering this evidence, malignancy risk does not appear to be significant with long-term IL-1ra use. Generalizability limitations include follow-up duration, as prolonged IL-1 inhibition might trigger cancer in genetically predisposed individuals. Nevertheless, in certain cases, oncological consultation is invaluable for assessing recurrence risk and increasing confidence in IL-1ra use for suitable patients.
